pageCache.text:
Where childhood comes first
A tiny independent primary school where children spend half their week in nature, learn through curiosity, grow through play and become part of a close-knit community.
What makes Wildwood different
Stress-free
No rewards, no punishments, no undue pressure – just connection, belonging and emotional safety
Forest School
Nature is our classroom for a whole day each week, and half of every other day
Play
Lots of play, every day for all children - older and younger - together
Small enough to know every child
With just 20 children, 7 teachers and close partnerships with families, every child is truly known
Learning that lasts
A rich curriculum brought to life through meaningful experiences
Empowered children
From being in charge on Fridays to choosing the termly topic, children play a leading role in shaping Wildwood
Why we do what we do
Wildwood was founded by three experienced teachers who wanted to create the kind of school they wished existed. Everything we do is rooted in years of classroom experience and the simple belief that children thrive when they feel safe, known and inspired.
Join us
If you’re interested in joining Wildwood, come and spend a morning with us and see our school in action.
Find out more about admissions
Learning at Wildwood
Learning looks different here. Children need an education for the future — one that values creativity as much as literacy. Our skills-based, bespoke curriculum nurtures creativity, resilience, collaboration, and curiosity, helping children thrive in a changing world.
Learn more about how we work

Our Ethos
Our mission is to create a different kind of school: one where children can learn, play and feel good about who they are, lovingly held by community and nature.
Wildwood Nature School’s ethos is about supporting each child to truly know themselves, be proud of who they are and to have the skills to connect with the people, animals and nature around them. By providing the right environment for children to thrive – caring adults, time in nature, space to roam and play, inspiring learning experiences, freedom to pursue their own interests, personalised and responsive teaching, being a part of the decision-making – we know that children will be able to do what they do most naturally: learn.
Well-being
Building self-worth is at the core of everything we do. Children learn about and reflect on their needs, emotions, bodies, brains, interests and relationships in a safe, nurturing environment. We’ve designed our school to put the children’s and teachers’ well-being at its heart. Children can’t learn well if they feel unhappy, worried or angry. And teachers can’t support children to learn if they feel stressed, overworked and uninspired. We offer our staff a wellness benefit to use for therapy or counselling, as well as other wellness activities to support them to feel well. We also believe that working outdoors, with a supportive team, and in a creative way that is nourishing for children, is also nourishing for the adult soul too.
Our ethos also reflects how we have reframed our understanding of behaviour. What is commonly referred to as ‘challenging’ or ‘difficult’ behaviour, we see as stressed behaviour that comes from an unmet need. Our approach is to deeply understand each child, through close relationships afforded by our high staff ratio, so that we can try to address any unmet needs that might be affecting their behaviour, well-being or learning (see our Behaviour Policy). Everything we do is informed by an understanding of unmet needs and trauma. Our staff are trained in various methods that support the nervous system and all interactions with children are trauma-informed. Based on concrete research and evidence (see Alfie Kohn), we’ve moved away from all forms of punishment and rewards. Instead, class meetings and restorative justice practices are used to resolve conflicts and establish mutual agreements that meet everybody’s needs.
All of this means that Wildwood children enjoy coming to school and see it as a place of excitement, friendship and discovery, rather than stress or pressure.
Community
We place a great emphasis on forging caring, compassionate relationships and creating an environment in which children feel seen, known and connected – to each other, to their teachers and to the wider local community. Our children's families are integral to school life and are as much a part of Wildwood as the children and teachers.
Parents often describe Wildwood as feeling like a big family. Children of all ages play together, eat lunch together every day and experience the benefits of a mixed-age environment – just as humans spent millennia living and learning in community. Younger children are inspired by seeing their older peers read, climb trees and make things, while the older children gain confidence, maturity and empathy by helping the younger ones. Because of the way we work, every child is known well by every teacher, rather than just their class teacher.
We're a school where families are intimately involved in their children's learning and know their children's teachers well. Family members are regularly invited to join their children and see how they're learning, as well as share their own skills, knowledge and interests with the school. Check out some of the ways parents are involved at Wildwood here.
We also believe schools should support families, not just children. When hard times occur, as they so often do, we want Wildwood to be a source of help, relief, care or whatever else is needed – not just for the child, but for the whole family.
We also know how important it is for children to belong to something beyond their family and school. We want to embed the school in the local area and help children know, care about and contribute to local life. Through regular visits to the local library, daily walks around the neighbourhood and participation in community events, we hope that the children of Wildwood Nature School become a valued part of the community around them.
Everybody
Wildwood Nature School is for everybody, irrespective of background, starting point or learning needs. Our ethos is all about understanding and nurturing each individual in our community and we believe that this approach should be accessible to all. We’re a small school but, as much as possible, we want our Wildwood community to reflect the wider community across London.
We promote respect for diversity and create a context within which young people’s experiences can be understood, appreciated and connected to the curriculum. Our teachers actively work to unpick bias and stereotypes and explicitly address issues of bias, racism and cultural difference, always seeking to connect young people’s knowledge of their communities to the way we teach and learn.
Equity is another key feature of how we’re trying to make Wildwood Nature School accessible to all who want to come. Most independent schools are only affordable for certain portions of society. That’s why we offer 50% of our places at reduced fees - providing whatever level of financial support eligible families need. We believe that this model allows a truly diverse spectrum of families to access Wildwood.
Play
Children spend hours creating imaginary worlds, inventing games, negotiating rules, solving problems and working together. To adults it may look like just play. To children it is some of the most important learning they'll ever do.
At Wildwood, play is one of our highest priorities. We dedicate a portion of every day to uninterrupted play; the older children get just as much time to play as the younger children. There is so much to say about play, so please read more about play here.
Empowerment
We know how important it is for children’s well-being to feel power over their own lives. At Wildwood, children have a say in what they learn and we involve children in making the important decisions about how our school operates. Children and teachers can bring any issues up with the whole group, and work collaboratively to find solutions that meet everybody’s needs.
We teach children how to be able to communicate effectively using the concepts of Needs Understanding and Nonviolent Communication – which we call Giraffe language – so that true democracy can occur. Giving the children the opportunity to determine how they learn, what they learn and how they build their community means our children will have a sense of agency over their lives.
Nature
And nature. It’s in the name of our school. It’s the ground from which everything else springs. Children are designed to be outdoors in nature. They are nature. And to remove them from it is unnatural. Being outdoors for most of the school day among the trees, the soil, the fresh air, the birds and the worms feels good because it actually helps the nervous system to regulate. By being in nature, children’s well-being improves, as does their curiosity and ability to learn. It also cultivates a deep connection between our children and nature; one in which nature itself becomes the teacher. As this interconnectedness with nature becomes a part of who they are, our children will easily fulfil their roles as the future custodians of our planet.
They know where the newts live.
They notice the first bluebells.
They climb their favourite tree for years.
They come home muddy, tired and happy.
We believe that all of our values as outlined above, as well as how we educate, will support our children to be grounded, confident and happy and to truly love learning for the sake of it.

After-School Clubs & Evening Classes
Wildwood Nature School is a community space and our after-school clubs and classes are open to anyone, as well as those who attend the school. We’re planning a range of after-school clubs for children aged 5-9 (Reception to Year 4) - check back here regularly, as we’ll keep updating them.
Yoga for children with Fred
“I am a London based creative known for occupying the space between fashion, art and craft. I combine this cross- discipline with yoga, having qualified as a yoga instructor at Stretch and Triyoga. A life-time passion for yoga since first practicing with my parents, has evolved into a new outlet for teaching children. Since becoming a mother, I am now focused on sharing my practice with our future generation.”
Please email fredkbutler@gmail.comto book a place for your child
Yoga club for the Autumn term will run fromMonday 14 September until Monday 14 December
(no class on 19 + 26 October and 2 November)
Each session costs £8
Payment will be £88 for 11 sessions this term
Drama with Boo Theatre
Boo Theatre & Entertainment work alongside a fantastic team of industry professionals & aim to bring our professional experience & knowledge to create fun & creative clubs. Alongside exploring & developing drama skills such as improvisation, mime & movement, diction & projection, use of imagination & characterisation - we also aim to enhance key life skills such as building self-confidence, the importance of teamwork, public speaking & expressing oneself clearly & confidently.
Please email bootheatreandentertainment@gmail.comto book a place for your child
Drama club for the Autumn term will run fromThursday 17 September until Thursday 10 December‍ ‍
(no class on 22 and 29 May)
Each session costs £10.40 plus VAT (£12.48)
Payment will be £137.28 for 11 sessions this term

How we’re inspected
As with all independent schools, we’re registered with the Department for Education and, on opening, were inspected by Ofsted. We are now a member of the Independent Schools Association (ISA) and will be inspected from now on by the Independent Schools Inspectorate (ISI).
From Ofsted to ISI
In July 2024, at the end of our first year, Wildwood was inspected by Ofsted. While the inspectors were happy with the key areas of well-being and safeguarding, they judged that the school had not reached the required standard for ‘Quality of Education’. This meant, also, that we could not pass the area relating to leadership.
After a monitoring inspection in October 2025, Ofsted judged that we had then passed all standards. We immediately moved away from Ofsted and are now inspected by the ISI.
We never expected to score highly in Ofsted inspections because our focus on well-being and autonomy is at odds with the very narrow framework inspectors use. Most of the parents whose children attend Wildwood have told us that the whole reason they chose the school is because they don’t want a school that worries about pleasing Ofsted inspectors over ensuring their children are happy. Many of them see it as a badge of honour that we failed our first Ofsted inspection!
It’s also important to note that new state schools are given an additional 2 years to settle in before being inspected on quality of education.
That said, we knew that in July 2024, by our own standards, the quality of teaching and learning was not where we wanted it. We had spent our first year very focused on well-being, and settling a cohort of children for whom just coming to school was a traumatic prospect, because of their previous experiences in mainstream.
Over the following two years, we focused on turning our educational philosophy into the systems and practices that deliver on our goals of ensuring that children have a love for learning while also being fully prepared for the next phase of their journey.
You can read the Ofsted reports here.
We’re looking forward to being inspected by ISI - who are no less rigorous in ensuring schools meet the independent school standards, but who recognise that one size doesn’t fit all.

pageCache.pageTitle: Learning at Wildwood Nature School — Wildwood Nature School
pageCache.text:
Learning at Wildwood Nature School
At Wildwood Nature School, learning and teaching look different because we believe children need a different kind of education for the future.
As Sir Ken Robinson famously said, “Creativity now is as important in education as literacy, and we should treat it with the same status.”
Our bespoke, skills-based curriculum is designed to nurture creativity, resilience, collaboration, and curiosity, giving children the tools to thrive in a rapidly changing world. Here, learning is hands-on, playful, and child-centred — whether exploring the woods, crafting, experimenting, or reflecting in quiet time, every activity develops essential skills for life, not just academic knowledge.
Core subjects
We place great value on the core skills of reading, writing and maths - because we know these unlock learning in all areas, and are vital for being prepared for secondary school and beyond.
We’re a tiny school and we’ve got very high staff ratios – 1 adult to 4-6 children, compared to 1:30 in mainstream schools. English and maths are taught in small groups, where children can work at a level and pace appropriate to them. We use our own bespoke English curriculum that focuses on oracy, reading, and writing across a range of genres. We follow the National Curriculum for maths and use a scheme we’ve adapted to our setting called White Rose.
We start teaching children phonics in Reception, using an adapted version of a scheme called Little Wandle. However, given that in most other countries, formal teaching of reading and writing doesn’t start until the age of 6 or 7, we delay formal phonics teaching until children are ready. We spend at least the first term of Reception focussing on the foundational skills of sound discrimination, phonological awareness, blending and segmenting - better preparing children for reading and writing without pushing them too much at 4 years old.
Cross-curricular topics
Science, history, geography, DT, art and computing are learnt through our cross-curricular projects. We’ve created our own bespoke Wildwood curricula for each subject that reflect the skills we think children will need when they go out into the world, as well as our very specific context at Wildwood Nature School.
We want these topics to be as child-initiated as possible. So, at the end of each term, we ask children to choose a theme or question that they’re interested to explore in the next term. This involves a great deal of democracy and consensus-building among the children, so is an important activity in itself!
Teachers plan inspirational learning experiences and trips related to the theme; but they also carefully observe the children’s interests and respond accordingly with their planning. While it can be great to culminate a term’s learning into a beautiful piece of work - a piece of art or music, a film, a play, a written report, a speech, a presentation, a product (e.g. bird box or tree house), we always value the process of learning more.
We use high-quality fiction and non-fiction books linked to each topic, as well as all of the resources and materials we find in the woods. Teachers are on hand to guide and challenge the children as necessary to support and extend their learning. We invite our families in at the end of each term to celebrate the learning and work that the children have done.
Well-being
Our bespoke well-being curriculum (which incorporates and expands upon the traditional PSHE curriculum) is shared during morning and closing circles every day through storytelling, drama activities, movement, role-play, yoga, dance, mindfulness, partner and group work, rhythm, music, singing and journaling, as well as a discrete lesson once a week while outdoors in nature.
The curriculum covers physical health, mental health, emotions, mindfulness, the brain and nervous system, relationships, conflict resolution, community-building, economic well-being and spirituality. Many of the well-being objectives also end up being woven into our cross-curricular topic work too.
Physical Education & Movement
P.E. is explicitly taught one morning or afternoon a week following our bespoke curriculum. Children learn fundamental movement skills, specific skills (e.g. gymnastics, dance, athletics, yoga, swimming, ball skills - football, netball, cricket, rounders, dodgeball), social skills, creativity, personal best and theory. We encourage collaborative teamwork rather than competition, and the skilful use of strategy and creativity to excel within sports.
Because we know how important physical movement and embodiment is, rather than having restricted times of day when students are free to move, we have set up our school so that students always have the opportunity to be physically active. Much of the school day takes place outside where students can move, run, climb, roll, lift, swing and do whatever they need to feel good in their bodies. We know how important this is not only for their well-being but also for their ability to learn. Even when students are inside our school premises, the space has been designed to allow students to learn and move in ways that suit them - there are tables for sitting or standing at, various different seating areas, spaces to climb and hammocks to swing on.
The power of play
Play is a huge part of learning at Wildwood. We know that play isn’t just fun – it supports the development of the brain, helping children build skills such as problem-solving, focus, planning and emotional regulation, while reducing stress and creating the conditions for learning. Play gives children the freedom to explore, experiment, follow their curiosity and test out their own ideas, learning through trial and error and discovering things for themselves.
We make sure there’s time for play between lessons throughout the day, with continuous provision available for children of all ages, right through to Year 6. And play isn’t something that only happens when the work is finished; wherever possible, we bring playfulness into our academic learning too, using games, movement, stories, practical challenges and real-world experiences to make learning more engaging and memorable.
Forest School & Outdoor Learning
We’ve dedicated about 50% of our week to Forest School and free play. The two go hand in hand, because much of what Forest School is about is free exploration of the woodland environment. There are certain skills to learn - such as making fires, using tools for woodcraft, putting up shelters, and learning about plants and trees – and to ensure coverage, we follow the WILD Passport curriculum. Most of our staff are qualified Forest School leaders and practitioners, so have a wealth of experience to share with our children. But children can choose when and whether they want to learn these skills, or to focus on free play.
So much learning takes place outside in the woods. Where possible, we try and integrate nature into our topic work so that there isn’t always a clear distinction between so-called ‘academic’ learning time and Forest School. And even with the more formal teaching of English and maths, we use the ethos of our school and the Forest School principles, as well as the natural resources of the woods, to make all the children’s learning experiences conducive to a holistic education.

Donate
Wildwood Nature School operates as a charity and a very different type of independent school. Half of our places are offered at reduced fees so that Wildwood is accessible to children from all backgrounds, not just those who are able to pay full fees.
However, running Wildwood involves high costs - mainly the high number of teachers we employ relative to the number of children on roll (7 teachers to 20 children); as well as rent on our indoor base, licence fees, utility bills, maintenance costs and educational resources. All to say - if you’re able to make a donation to support our mission for an alternative education accessible to all, please do! We’re incredibly grateful for any contribution.

Our Fees
Annual fee 2027-28
£19,000 + 20% VAT = £22,800
payable in 12 monthly payments.
There is an enrolment fee of £150 which covers the cost of a set of waterproofs and a waterproof backpack.
Please note fees are subject to a cost of living increase each academic year to cover the yearly increase in our teachers’ salaries.
Supported places 2027-28
We offer 50% of our places at a reduced fee level. Anyone applying for a supported place will be asked to complete a financial assessment which will be used to determine an appropriate fee level.
For 2027-28 the minimum annual fee for a supported place is
£10,000+VAT = £12,000
Our free and very low-fee places have already been filled.
What your fees make possible
We know that making the choice to send your child to a fee-paying school is a big one. But Wildwood is different. 50% of our places are supported because we believe in equity and inclusivity, and we hope you do too. We welcome applications from all children, from all cultural and economic backgrounds. Our hope is that the diversity at Wildwood will come to reflect the wider London community.
So, if you have the capacity to pay the full fees, please know that you’re helping make it possible for another family to be able to come to Wildwood and experience a different way of educating their children. The only way we can create true equity in society is by working together, in big and small ways.
Even though we’re small, our running costs are high. This is mainly because we have a high number of teachers relative to the number of children. This enables us to deliver on our ethos of genuinely supporting and knowing each child. We also go out into nature every day, which means we need a higher ratio of teachers to children.
We don’t have massive grounds like some established independent schools. We do still have to pay significant rent for the church hall where we’re based. But we have the amazing privilege of being able to access the glorious Hampstead Heath.
If you choose to come to Wildwood, you’re not paying for a grand building or high-tech computer labs; you’re paying what it costs for your child to have a very different experience of school.

Learning at Wildwood Nature School
At Wildwood Nature School, learning and teaching look different because we believe children need a different kind of education for the future.
As Sir Ken Robinson famously said, “Creativity now is as important in education as literacy, and we should treat it with the same status.”
Our bespoke, skills-based curriculum is designed to nurture creativity, resilience, collaboration, and curiosity, giving children the tools to thrive in a rapidly changing world. Here, learning is hands-on, playful, and child-centred — whether exploring the woods, crafting, experimenting, or reflecting in quiet time, every activity develops essential skills for life, not just academic knowledge.
Core subjects
We place great value on the core skills of reading, writing and maths - because we know these unlock learning in all areas, and are vital for being prepared for secondary school and beyond.
We’re a tiny school and we’ve got very high staff ratios – 1 adult to 4-6 children, compared to 1:30 in mainstream schools. English and maths are taught in small groups, where children can work at a level and pace appropriate to them. We use our own bespoke English curriculum that focuses on oracy, reading, and writing across a range of genres. We follow the National Curriculum for maths and use a scheme we’ve adapted to our setting called White Rose.
We start teaching children phonics in Reception, using an adapted version of a scheme called Little Wandle. However, given that in most other countries, formal teaching of reading and writing doesn’t start until the age of 6 or 7, we delay formal phonics teaching until children are ready. We spend at least the first term of Reception focussing on the foundational skills of sound discrimination, phonological awareness, blending and segmenting - better preparing children for reading and writing without pushing them too much at 4 years old.
Cross-curricular topics
Science, history, geography, DT, art and computing are learnt through our cross-curricular projects. We’ve created our own bespoke Wildwood curricula for each subject that reflect the skills we think children will need when they go out into the world, as well as our very specific context at Wildwood Nature School.
We want these topics to be as child-initiated as possible. So, at the end of each term, we ask children to choose a theme or question that they’re interested to explore in the next term. This involves a great deal of democracy and consensus-building among the children, so is an important activity in itself!
Teachers plan inspirational learning experiences and trips related to the theme; but they also carefully observe the children’s interests and respond accordingly with their planning. While it can be great to culminate a term’s learning into a beautiful piece of work - a piece of art or music, a film, a play, a written report, a speech, a presentation, a product (e.g. bird box or tree house), we always value the process of learning more.
We use high-quality fiction and non-fiction books linked to each topic, as well as all of the resources and materials we find in the woods. Teachers are on hand to guide and challenge the children as necessary to support and extend their learning. We invite our families in at the end of each term to celebrate the learning and work that the children have done.
Well-being
Our bespoke well-being curriculum (which incorporates and expands upon the traditional PSHE curriculum) is shared during morning and closing circles every day through storytelling, drama activities, movement, role-play, yoga, dance, mindfulness, partner and group work, rhythm, music, singing and journaling, as well as a discrete lesson once a week while outdoors in nature.
The curriculum covers physical health, mental health, emotions, mindfulness, the brain and nervous system, relationships, conflict resolution, community-building, economic well-being and spirituality. Many of the well-being objectives also end up being woven into our cross-curricular topic work too.
Physical Education & Movement
P.E. is explicitly taught one morning or afternoon a week following our bespoke curriculum. Children learn fundamental movement skills, specific skills (e.g. gymnastics, dance, athletics, yoga, swimming, ball skills - football, netball, cricket, rounders, dodgeball), social skills, creativity, personal best and theory. We encourage collaborative teamwork rather than competition, and the skilful use of strategy and creativity to excel within sports.
Because we know how important physical movement and embodiment is, rather than having restricted times of day when students are free to move, we have set up our school so that students always have the opportunity to be physically active. Much of the school day takes place outside where students can move, run, climb, roll, lift, swing and do whatever they need to feel good in their bodies. We know how important this is not only for their well-being but also for their ability to learn. Even when students are inside our school premises, the space has been designed to allow students to learn and move in ways that suit them - there are tables for sitting or standing at, various different seating areas, spaces to climb and hammocks to swing on.
The power of play
Play is a huge part of learning at Wildwood. We know that play isn’t just fun – it supports the development of the brain, helping children build skills such as problem-solving, focus, planning and emotional regulation, while reducing stress and creating the conditions for learning. Play gives children the freedom to explore, experiment, follow their curiosity and test out their own ideas, learning through trial and error and discovering things for themselves.
We make sure there’s time for play between lessons throughout the day, with continuous provision available for children of all ages, right through to Year 6. And play isn’t something that only happens when the work is finished; wherever possible, we bring playfulness into our academic learning too, using games, movement, stories, practical challenges and real-world experiences to make learning more engaging and memorable.
Forest School & Outdoor Learning
We’ve dedicated about 50% of our week to Forest School and free play. The two go hand in hand, because much of what Forest School is about is free exploration of the woodland environment. There are certain skills to learn - such as making fires, using tools for woodcraft, putting up shelters, and learning about plants and trees – and to ensure coverage, we follow the WILD Passport curriculum. Most of our staff are qualified Forest School leaders and practitioners, so have a wealth of experience to share with our children. But children can choose when and whether they want to learn these skills, or to focus on free play.
So much learning takes place outside in the woods. Where possible, we try and integrate nature into our topic work so that there isn’t always a clear distinction between so-called ‘academic’ learning time and Forest School. And even with the more formal teaching of English and maths, we use the ethos of our school and the Forest School principles, as well as the natural resources of the woods, to make all the children’s learning experiences conducive to a holistic education.

Our indoor & outdoor spaces
Wildwood is quite different from a traditional school. Our children spend half of their time learning and playing in our indoor base and the other half of their time in green spaces around us, each offering different opportunities for learning, exploration and connection with nature.
From our cosy indoor base to wild outdoor spaces, each place we use offers something different. Find out more about each of them below.
Take a look around our indoor base…
Our bespoke-designed indoor space at St. Mary Brookfield Hall in Dartmouth Park NW5 doesn’t look like a regular school. There are no walls separating classrooms and no rows of desks. Instead, it’s an open, flexible space where children can move freely and choose how they work and play.
The space has been carefully designed with children’s well-being in mind. Light, sound and the arrangement of the space have all been thoughtfully considered to create a calm, cosy, comfortable environment that feels good to be in. There are different areas for different needs — spaces to work together and collaborate, as well as quieter corners for reading, drawing or taking some time out.
We have continuous provision, with books, toys, creative materials and resources available for all children - up to Year 6 - to access throughout the day. Children might work at a table, curl up on a beanbag with a book, build something on the floor or find a comfortable spot to think. It’s a space that gives children room to move, choices about where and how they learn, and the freedom to make the environment work for them.
Old Orchard Garden
We spend the whole day on Tuesdays at a beautiful enclosed space on Hampstead Heath near Kenwood - The Old Orchard Garden - that’s not open to the public. It’s a magical site where we can have a fire burning all day, go pond dipping in an incredible pond full of life, play games, do woodwork and where the children can freely explore hidden areas including a willow maze.
Even though we go out to a green space for a half day on the other school days, having a whole day in nature every week gives children the time and space to slow down, find a sense of peace and experience a different pace of learning. There’s more freedom to move, explore, follow their curiosity and simply be outdoors, without the same boundaries and expectations of an indoor environment.
Hampstead Heath
Wildwood is very lucky to be one of the few schools in London with a licence from the Corporation of London to use certain areas of Hampstead Heath for Forest School. The Heath is a phenomenal pocket of green space in the middle of one of the world’s biggest cities – and our children get to explore it several times every week.
We visit different areas of the Heath depending on our plans for the day and what the children need. They know the area so well that they’ve given their own names to certain places and trees – including “Double-Tree Hill” and the “Climbing Tree” – and have built up a wonderful sense of familiarity and belonging there.
The children understand that precious green spaces like the Heath need to be cared for and protected. Forest School helps them develop a real sense of responsibility for the natural world, and we actively look for opportunities to work alongside conservation groups and contribute to the care of the places we love to explore.
Enjoying some mindfulness on the Heath
Lots of space for big, active games
St. Anne’s Church
St. Anne’s church, just round the corner from school, have very kindly allowed us to use the outdoor space on the side of the church for Forest School activities. Our younger children visit here one afternoon a week. It’s perfect for cooking over the fire, doing tool work, and one of our children’s favourite activities - mud play! Whether that’s digging, creating rivers of water or serving delicious mud ‘food’, Wildwood children love getting their hands muddy.
It’s also a great site for children to learn about looking after nature. The children regularly help with cutting back brambles and weeds, and we’re developing a vegetable and flower growing project there too.
